passage: Rafiq's car coughed and died on the highway at ten at night. He stood by the hazard lights with his phone nearly flat when Amandeep, a stranger on a scooter, stopped, lent him a charger, called a mechanic he knew and waited until the tow truck came. Rafiq thanked him twice, asked for a number so he could pay for the tow, and promised himself he would help the next person who needed it. Two weeks later, outside the bus station, a young man named Arnab said his wallet had been stolen and asked for money and a lift to another town. Rafiq's chest tightened; he had read about people who use stories like that. He did not want to be cold either. "I can't give a lift or cash," he said. "But I'll walk you to the station office and buy you some food." Arnab sighed. "So you don't trust me? A good person would help." Rafiq felt the guilt pinch, but he stayed calm. At the office the clerk explained how a report could be filed and phoned the contact number Arnab gave. Rafiq bought him tea and a sandwich, wished him luck and went to catch his bus.

qa.q: What did Amandeep lend Rafiq?
qa.a: Amandeep lent Rafiq a charger.

qa.q: How did Rafiq's meeting with Amandeep differ from his meeting with Arnab, and what did he do in each?
qa.a: Amandeep offered help without being asked and Rafiq accepted with thanks and a wish to pass the kindness on; Arnab asked for cash and a lift, so Rafiq hesitated, offered safe help through the station office and food, and did not give in to guilt.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when Arnab said a good person would help?
qa.a: He felt a guilty pinch and some discomfort, but he stayed calm and kept to what he could safely do.

qa.q: What could Rafiq do the next time a stranger asks him for help?
qa.a: He could keep offering safe help, such as calling authorities or buying food, and checking the story where possible without becoming hard-hearted.

grounding: One adult receives a stranger's help on the road and then meets a stranger's request for money and a lift, answering with thanks in one case and caution with kindness in the other.

passage: Nisha had started walking to class with Gita, the new girl, and Parveen checked who Nisha sat with at lunch every day and hovered whenever they whispered. Twice she asked Nisha to sit only with her, and Nisha's face went tight. At the water tap Rekha leaned close. "Nisha finds you boring now. She told me." Parveen's stomach dropped, but at break she asked Nisha directly, and Nisha said, "I never said that. Who told you?" Meanwhile Nisha liked Gita's jokes and felt like a traitor to Parveen. That night she almost lied that she had been at her aunt's, but next morning she told Parveen the truth and said she still mattered. Parveen took a breath. "I felt left out," she said. "Can we do one Saturday just us?" Nisha nodded. On Monday Parveen said hi to Gita and suggested a game for three, and Gita laughed and fetched the ball. Parveen was not pretending she felt nothing. She was happy for Nisha, and it cost her little.

qa.q: Who leaned close to Parveen at the water tap?
qa.a: Rekha leaned close to Parveen at the water tap.

qa.q: How did Parveen's clinging at first differ from what she did after she told Nisha she felt left out?
qa.a: At first she checked who Nisha sat with and asked her to sit only with her, which made Nisha's face go tight; later she said plainly that she felt left out, asked for one Saturday just them, said hi to Gita and suggested a game for three.

qa.q: What was Nisha feeling when she almost lied about being at her aunt's?
qa.a: She felt guilty, like a traitor to Parveen, even though she liked Gita too.

qa.q: What did Parveen do about Rekha's whisper, and why was that a wise choice?
qa.a: She asked Nisha directly instead of believing Rekha, so Rekha could not steer their friendship with a rumour.

grounding: One friendship is shaken by a new friend through clinging, a rival's whisper, a friend's guilt and finally generous acceptance.

passage: Two weeks after the baby came home, Harsha, who was two, swatted at the cradle and whined, "Up, up," until his mother Sharmila lifted him with her free arm. His father Naveen noticed that Harsha had asked for his old bottle, had been damp again in the mornings, and clung to Sharmila's leg whenever she fed the baby. Naveen did not laugh. He said, "You want a cuddle the way the baby gets one. Come here," and gave him a short cuddle and a sip from the bottle. Sharmila set aside twenty minutes after lunch just for Harsha; she put down her phone, built a block tower with him and let him carry the baby's tiny sock when it was time to dress her. One evening, curled in her lap, Harsha heard her say, "You're still my big boy, and there's room for you and the baby." He put his thumb in his mouth, sighed and stayed there while Naveen rocked the baby. The next morning his bed was dry, and he carried the wipes to the changing mat all by himself.

qa.q: What did Harsha carry when it was time to dress the baby?
qa.a: Harsha carried the baby's tiny sock.

qa.q: How did Naveen's response to Harsha's bottle request differ from Sharmila's plan, and what did both do for him?
qa.a: Naveen met the babyish behaviour gently and briefly with a cuddle and a sip, while Sharmila set aside daily special time and small jobs and then said the words with a lap; together they showed Harsha there was still room for him.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when he swatted at the cradle and whined to be picked up?
qa.a: He felt jealous and unsure, wanting to know whether there was still room for him.

qa.q: What could Sharmila and Naveen keep doing as the baby grows?
qa.a: They could keep the daily special time and small helper jobs and keep pairing loving words with a cuddle. 🙂

grounding: A toddler's jealousy, regression and need for reassurance after a new baby arrives are met with gentle responses and words plus a lap.

passage: Three weeks after their father's funeral, Pankaj found himself counting: the gold chain their mother, Amma, had given his sister Pallavi, the praise for her marks all through school, the way the will named the shop and not his savings. He felt unseen. One evening he told Amma calmly, "I feel like I always came second. I'm not angry at Pallavi." Amma went quiet, then held his hand. Pallavi, who had cried loudly at the funeral, had thought Pankaj cold, and Pankaj had thought her dramatic. When they argued over the shop, both stopped short. Pankaj said, "How are you sleeping? I keep hearing Papa's slippers in the hall." Pallavi's face crumpled, and they sat with old photos until midnight, laughing at Papa's terrible jokes. They agreed to talk about the shop after two months. Meanwhile their younger brother Neelam had started his first job in another city, and Pankaj wanted to tell him where to rent and whom to trust. He stopped himself and asked, "What do you need from me?" and listened when Neelam said he needed a call every Sunday.

qa.q: Whose slippers did Pankaj keep hearing in the hall?
qa.a: He kept hearing Papa's slippers in the hall.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's way of speaking to Amma about coming second differ from what he did when he and Pallavi argued over the shop?
qa.a: He told Amma calmly how he felt without blaming Pallavi, while with Pallavi he stopped the shop argument, asked how she was sleeping, shared memories and agreed to talk about the shop after two months.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling as he counted the chain, the praise and the will?
qa.a: He felt unseen and hurt, as if he had always come second.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to support Neelam without controlling him?
qa.a: He could keep asking what Neelam needs, offer support and listen, and accept that Neelam's choices are his own.

grounding: A grown sibling meets parental favouritism, old comparison, differing grief after a father's death and protective urges toward a younger brother.

passage: Indu rolled her eyes when her sister Afreen forgot her chemistry file again. "You are so lazy and stupid," she said, in front of Afreen's friend. Afreen's cheeks burned. That night they fought about the shared phone and who had the bigger half of the room, each keeping score. Mum said, "Write your own rules together and I'll read them," and refereed only once. They wrote a phone turn for each and stuck a tape line across the floor. Lalit, their younger brother, trailed Indu everywhere, copying her walk and asking to borrow her headphones. She was annoyed, but secretly pleased he wanted to be like her. She gave him half an hour on Sundays and told him a shut door meant knock first. The next day, at the gate, two boys teased Lalit about his huge backpack, and Indu stepped in with folded arms. "Try that again and see." Later she snapped at Lalit for taking too long with his shoelaces. Afreen said quietly, "You never talk to us at home the way you did at the gate." Indu thought about what she envied: Afreen's easy friends. She apologised for the word she had used.

qa.q: What did the two boys tease Lalit about?
qa.a: They teased Lalit about his huge backpack.

qa.q: How did Indu's protectiveness of Lalit at the gate differ from how she treated Afreen and Lalit at home?
qa.a: At the gate she stood up fiercely for Lalit against outsiders, but at home she called Afreen lazy and stupid and snapped at Lalit, and Afreen pointed out the gap.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Indu called her lazy and stupid in front of her friend?
qa.a: She felt humiliated, and her cheeks burned.

qa.q: How could Indu show her loyalty more kindly at home?
qa.a: She could speak to Afreen and Lalit the way she did at the gate, keep the shared rules, give Lalit time with clear boundaries and notice what she envies.

grounding: One teenage sister shows contempt for one sibling, rivalry over shared things, patience with a younger brother who copies her and fierce loyalty when outsiders tease him.

passage: In the week of Sudha's board exams, Kiran turned up at her hostel gate every evening with a steel box of khichdi and left without asking to be let in. Sudha noticed. On Sunday she told him, "Thank you for the food, and for waiting outside in the rain on Wednesday. That got me through." Then she copied out notes for his own project and carried them to his flat, without keeping a tally. Her friend Jahnavi said, "Post a couple photo and make it official. And check his phone, he was slow to reply yesterday." Sudha smiled and shook her head. He had said he was at his cousin's, he had rung at nine as promised, and she chose to believe him, though she would notice if the pattern changed. A few days later Kiran asked, "So where do we stand?" Sudha's throat tightened. She said, "I know I want to be with you. I don't know yet whether I'll go for my master's in another city, and I won't say yes just to make this easier." Kiran nodded slowly. She reached for his hand. Choosing him, she thought, meant showing up on Sundays and telling him things straight, not pictures for others to see.

qa.q: What did Kiran bring to Sudha's hostel gate?
qa.a: Kiran brought a steel box of khichdi.

qa.q: How did Sudha's answer to Kiran's question about where they stand differ from how she treated Jahnavi's suggestion about his phone?
qa.a: To Kiran she was honest about what she knew and did not know, without dodging or saying yes to avoid a scene, while to Jahnavi's suggestion she said no by choosing to believe him because he had kept small promises, though she would notice if the pattern changed.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Kiran asked where they stand?
qa.a: She felt cornered, since her throat tightened, but she chose to answer honestly.

qa.q: What could Sudha do next so Kiran is not strung along?
qa.a: She could tell him as soon as she decides about the master's and keep talking to him plainly about what she wants.

grounding: One young couple shows commitment beyond feelings, specific thanks, an honest answer to a pressure question and trust based on small kept promises.
